title: GIDEON’S CONCUBINE GAVE BIRTH TO ABIMELECH—Who Later Murdered Nearly All His Brothers
paragraphs: GIDEON’S CONCUBINE GAVE BIRTH TO ABIMELECH—Who Later Murdered Nearly All His Brothers
Gideon defeated an enemy army with 300 men. But the enemy growing inside his own house would become one of the darkest consequences recorded in Judges.
There is something terrifying about surviving the battlefield… only to discover that the greater tragedy was growing quietly inside your own home.
Gideon had watched God reduce an army to three hundred men.
He had heard the trumpets.
Seen the torches.
Watched Midian collapse.
He had experienced the kind of supernatural victory most believers can only imagine.
And yet Judges does not end Gideon’s story with the victory.
It takes us home with him.
That is where the story becomes uncomfortable.
Because sometimes the greatest danger to a victorious believer is not the enemy he just defeated.
Sometimes it is what he allows after the victory.
Judges 8 tells us that Israel wanted Gideon to establish what amounted to a hereditary dynasty. Gideon answered with words that sounded wonderfully faithful:
“I will not rule over you, neither shall my son rule over you: the LORD shall rule over you.”
That was the right answer.
But what happened afterward complicates the picture.

Gideon accumulated enormous wealth. He possessed many wives. He fathered seventy sons. He made an ephod from the gold Israel had given him, and that ephod became a spiritual snare to Gideon and his household.
Then Scripture quietly introduces another woman.
And one child.
One verse.
Almost easy to overlook.
But that verse opens the door to one of the bloodiest family tragedies in the book of Judges.
“And his concubine that was in Shechem, she also bare him a son, whose name he called Abimelech.”
—Judges 8:31
The Hebrew is even more revealing.
וּפִילַגְשׁוֹ אֲשֶׁר בִּשְׁכֶם יָלְדָה־לּוֹ גַם־הִיא בֵּן וַיָּשֶׂם אֶת־שְׁמוֹ אֲבִימֶלֶךְ
Ufilagsho asher biShekhem yaldah-lo gam-hi ben, vayasem et-shemo Avimelekh.
His פִּילֶגֶשׁ — pilegesh, commonly translated “concubine,” who lived in Shechem bore him a son.
His name was אֲבִימֶלֶךְ — Avimelekh.
And the name itself is haunting.
Avi — “my father.”
Melekh — “king.”
“My father is king.”
Perhaps the name reflected status, aspiration, or something else—we should not pretend Scripture tells us Gideon’s motive when it does not.
But the irony is impossible to miss.
Gideon had publicly declared:
“The LORD shall rule over you.”
Yet from Gideon’s own household emerged a son whose story would become consumed with making himself king.
Read that slowly.
A father can say the right words publicly while still leaving contradictions privately.
A person can win battles for God and still leave doors unlocked in his own soul.
You can know how to fight Midian and still fail to recognize what pride, compromise, appetite, influence, money, or unchecked ambition is doing inside your house.
That should frighten every one of us enough to examine ourselves.
Because your greatest spiritual danger may not always arrive looking like an enemy.
Sometimes it grows from something you tolerated.
Sometimes it begins as a compromise nobody confronted.
Sometimes it hides behind success.
And sometimes the consequences do not fully appear until years later.
Gideon eventually died.
Israel again turned toward the Baals.
And then Abimelech moved.
He went to Shechem—to his mother’s relatives—and made his argument.
Why should seventy sons of Gideon rule when Shechem could have one man?
Me.
And then came the line every manipulator knows how to exploit:
Remember…
I am your flesh and blood.
Abimelech appealed to tribal loyalty.
Family loyalty.
Identity.
Self-interest.
He did not need to prove that he was righteous.
He only needed to convince people that he was one of them.
And it worked.
The leaders of Shechem gave him seventy pieces of silver.
But notice where the money came from.
The house of Baal-berith.
Money associated with an idolatrous sanctuary financed Abimelech’s rise.
Then Abimelech used that money to hire what Scripture describes as reckless and worthless men.
And they followed him.
Now imagine the road to Ophrah.
Imagine the footsteps.
Imagine Gideon’s sons seeing their half-brother coming.
Perhaps some recognized him.
Perhaps somebody smiled.
Perhaps somebody thought family had arrived.
They had no idea death was walking toward them.
Judges 9:5 says:
וַיַּהֲרֹג אֶת־אֶחָיו בְּנֵי־יְרֻבַּעַל שִׁבְעִים אִישׁ עַל־אֶבֶן אֶחָת
Vayahărog et-echav benei-Yerubbaal, shiv'im ish, al-even achat.
He killed his brothers—the sons of Jerubbaal—
“seventy men…”
עַל־אֶבֶן אֶחָת — al-even achat.
“Upon one stone.”
One stone.
Again.
And again.
And again.
The text gives us no sentimental description.
No dramatic speeches from the victims.
No attempt to soften what happened.
Just the brutal image:
brothers slaughtered upon one stone.

There is a numerical detail worth handling carefully. Judges describes Gideon as having seventy sons, speaks of Abimelech killing the seventy, and then immediately tells us that Jotham, the youngest, survived because he hid. The narrative therefore presents Jotham as the surviving brother from that group; the “seventy” functions as the stated family total while the text itself makes the exception explicit.
Jotham escaped.
Think about that.
While Abimelech was building a throne…
Jotham was hiding to stay alive.
One brother wanted everybody to see him.
The other survived because nobody could find him.
One was being celebrated.
The other was probably terrified.
And if you have ever watched somebody who hurt you appear to prosper while you were barely surviving what they did…
you understand something of the emotional tension here.
Sometimes evil looks successful before judgment arrives.
Sometimes the person who betrayed you appears to move forward while you are still collecting the broken pieces.
Sometimes manipulation gets applause.
Sometimes arrogance gets a platform.
Sometimes wickedness gets money, influence, followers, connections, and power.
And you wonder:
“God… did You see this?”
Judges 9 answers:
Yes.
God saw everything.
But Jotham did something extraordinary before disappearing.
He climbed Mount Gerizim and cried out to the people of Shechem.
Then he told them a story.
The trees wanted a king.
They approached the olive tree.
The olive refused.
They approached the fig tree.
The fig refused.
They approached the vine.
The vine refused.
Finally they approached the thornbush.
And the thornbush accepted.
That image is devastating.
The fruitful trees were already occupied producing something valuable.
But the bramble wanted the throne.
There is a warning here that reaches far beyond ancient Shechem.
Never confuse someone’s hunger for authority with God’s qualification for authority.
Not everyone desperate to lead is called to lead.
Not everyone demanding recognition carries fruit.
Not everybody who says, “Follow me,” has been sent by God.
Jesus later gave His disciples an entirely different vision of greatness.
The rulers of the Gentiles “lord it over” others, He said, but among His followers greatness would be expressed through service.
That is why Abimelech’s kingdom feels so different from the kingdom of Christ.
Abimelech climbed upward by killing his brothers.
Jesus descended in humility to save His brothers and sisters.
Abimelech spilled other people’s blood to obtain a throne.
Jesus spilled His own blood to rescue sinners.
Abimelech sacrificed others for himself.
Christ gave Himself for others.
Abimelech said, in effect:
“Let them die so I can reign.”
Jesus came declaring through His actions:
“I will die so they can live.”
Do you see the Gospel hiding against the darkness?
This is why the ugliest stories in Scripture still matter.
They show us what human beings become when sin rules without repentance.
Abimelech got his kingdom.
For a while.
Three years passed.
Three years can feel like forever when you are waiting for justice.
But Scripture says God sent division between Abimelech and the leaders of Shechem.
The alliance built on selfish ambition began devouring itself.
That is the nature of sin.
Sin promises partnership and eventually produces slavery.
It promises pleasure and eventually demands payment.
It promises control and eventually controls you.
It promises secrecy and eventually exposes you.
It whispers:
“Nobody will ever know.”
Then one day you discover that the thing you thought you controlled has become your master.
Maybe your battlefield is not Abimelech’s battlefield.
Maybe nobody knows yours.
Maybe it is pornography.
An affair.
Bitterness.
Pride.
Alcohol.
Gambling.
Secret messages.
Jealousy.
Greed.
A hidden relationship.
A second life online.
Hatred toward somebody who hurt you.
A religious image protecting an unrepentant heart.
You still post Bible verses.
Still say “God bless.”
Still worship.
Still smile.
But somewhere inside you there is an Abimelech demanding a throne that belongs to Jesus.
And that is where this ancient story suddenly stops being ancient.
Because Abimelech is not merely a monster for us to stare at from a safe distance.
His story forces us to confront the terrifying potential of the human heart when ambition, idolatry, pride, violence, and self-rule are allowed to reign.
You may never murder seventy brothers.
But have you destroyed someone with words because they stood between you and what you wanted?
Have you secretly enjoyed someone else’s failure?
Have you manipulated people?
Have you used relationships to advance yourself?
Have you demanded recognition?
Have you protected your reputation more fiercely than your holiness?
Have you wanted the throne?
Be honest.
This is where the Gospel becomes painfully beautiful.
Christianity does not teach that we are basically good people who occasionally make unfortunate mistakes.
Scripture goes deeper.
Our problem reaches the heart.
We need more than inspiration.
We need reconciliation.
Forgiveness.
A new heart.
A new King.
We need Jesus.
Abimelech kept going.
Violence escalated.
Shechem eventually burned.
About a thousand men and women died in the tower of Shechem.
Then Abimelech marched against Thebez.
There was another tower.
People fled inside.
Abimelech approached its entrance, apparently intending to burn it as he had done before.
He had done this before.
It had worked before.
Perhaps he assumed it would work again.
But somewhere above him stood an unnamed woman.
Not a warrior whose biography Scripture celebrates.
Not a king.
Not a famous judge.
The Bible does not even give us her name.
She had an upper millstone.
And she dropped it.
The stone struck Abimelech’s head.
His skull was crushed.
The man who had slaughtered his brothers upon one stone was brought down beneath a stone.
And even while dying, Abimelech remained obsessed with his reputation.
He ordered his armor-bearer to kill him because he did not want people saying:
“A woman killed him.”
Imagine it.
His skull was shattered.
His kingdom was collapsing.
Death was seconds away.
And he was still worried about what people would say about him.
That may be one of the saddest portraits of pride anywhere in Scripture.
He was dying…
and still managing his image.
And suddenly the story asks us another uncomfortable question:
How much of your life is being spent trying to control what people think about you?
How much energy goes into appearing strong?
Appearing successful?
Appearing spiritual?
Appearing happy?
Appearing healed?
Appearing holy?
Maybe you are exhausted because you have been protecting an image Jesus never asked you to maintain.
Maybe repentance begins when you finally stop saying,
“What will people think?”
and start asking,
“What does God see?”
Because God already knows.
The secret.
The addiction.
The anger.
The compromise.
The night nobody knows about.
The message you deleted.
The tears you hid.
The resentment you buried.
The prayer life that disappeared.
The faith that feels weaker than everyone thinks it is.
He knows.
And somehow the Gospel still says:
Come.
Not because sin is insignificant.
But because the blood of Jesus is sufficient.
The final verses of Judges 9 make the theological meaning unmistakable.
God brought Abimelech’s evil back upon him, and the wickedness of Shechem returned upon its people.
Jotham’s warning had not vanished into the wind.
God had heard.
God had seen.
Justice had not been asleep.
But if all we learn from Abimelech is “bad people eventually get punished,” we have stopped too early.
Because you and I need more than justice against people worse than ourselves.
We need mercy for ourselves.
At the cross, justice and mercy meet.
Jesus does not excuse sin.
He bears judgment against sin.
He does not tell sinners to hide more successfully.
He calls sinners into the light.
He does not merely improve people.
He saves.
The Gospel says that the throne belongs to Someone entirely unlike Abimelech.
A King who wore thorns instead of becoming one.
A King who did not murder His brothers to protect His throne.
A King whose enemies mocked Him while He prayed for forgiveness.
A King who carried a cross.
A King who entered death.
A King who rose again.
Jesus Christ.
And perhaps that is what someone reading this needs right now.
Not another religious performance.
Not another promise that you will “do better.”
Not another week pretending everything is fine.
Repent.
Come home.
Tell Jesus the truth you think He does not already know.
Bring Him the hidden thing.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the pride.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the bitterness.
Bring Him the part of you that keeps reaching for the throne.
The Gospel is not God saying your sin never mattered.
The Gospel is God showing just how much it mattered—
and then showing the immeasurable price Christ willingly paid to redeem sinners.
Grace is not permission to remain Abimelech.
Grace is Christ rescuing us from the kingdom of self and bringing us under His righteous reign.
Maybe this article exposed something.
There are moments when three words can become the first crack in a wall you have spent years building.
Not because every paragraph will be comfortable to reread.
God sees what is hidden.
Sin never makes a trustworthy king.
Jesus still receives repentant sinners.
And grace can rewrite what shame convinced you was already finished.
Not merely to increase numbers.
There may be an Abimelech slowly surrendering to ambition, bitterness, lust, pride, or secret sin.
There may be a Jotham hiding somewhere, wondering whether God saw what happened.
There may be someone smiling in photographs tonight while privately asking God whether life is still worth fighting for.
You may never know whose screen this reaches because you pressed Share.
Send it privately to the believer who has gone quiet.
Send it to the person who stopped attending church.
Send it to the person who thinks his scandal has disqualified him forever.
Send it even to the skeptic who thinks Christianity is about pretending Christians never fail.
The Bible does not hide the scandal.
It reveals what sin does—
and then points us toward the grace we desperately need.

Supporting Gospel ministry financially should never be presented as purchasing God’s favor, buying salvation, or replacing obedience to Christ. Scripture teaches willing, cheerful generosity—not giving under compulsion.
And there is another reason to stay connected.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite the struggling believer.
Invite the lukewarm Christian.
Invite the seeker.
Invite the person who does not yet believe.
But never confuse supporting a ministry with supporting the Gospel itself.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
Grace is not merchandise.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
Your support simply helps put that message in front of another human being.
Gideon once stood before Israel after an astonishing victory and declared that the LORD should rule over them.
Yet within a generation, his own son reached for a throne.
Abimelech murdered for it.
Manipulated for it.
Destroyed people for it.
Killed brothers for it.
Burned cities for it.
And when death finally found him, he was still protecting his reputation.
Do not wait until everything collapses before surrendering your throne.
There is only one King who can carry the weight of your life.
His name is Jesus.
Give Him the secret.
Give Him the reputation.
Give Him the ambition.
Give Him the wound.
Give Him the past.
Give Him the future.
Give Him the throne.
Because the most frightening part of Abimelech’s story is not that a wicked man once wanted to become king.
It is realizing how desperately the human heart still wants to become its own king.
And the most beautiful part of the Gospel is that Jesus does not merely expose the rebel hiding inside us.
He died for rebels.
He forgives rebels who repent.
He transforms rebels who surrender.
And He makes sons and daughters out of people whose stories looked beyond redemption.
So before you leave this page, ask yourself one question you cannot answer casually:
Who is really sitting on the throne of my life?
If the answer exposes you, do not run from Jesus.
Run to Him.
Because sometimes the stone that shatters your illusion is the mercy that finally drives you back to the King.
